title: The prodigal son
hookLine: a father runs down the road to a son who wasted everything (Luke 15:11–32)

cards: There's a message people put off sending. The one to someone they let down, or drifted from, or said something to that they regret. It gets drafted in the head a dozen times.
Hey, I know it's been a while. I know I messed up. The apology gets rehearsed until it's perfect, along with every way it could go wrong.
Jesus told a story about a young man doing exactly that, rehearsing his apology the whole long walk home. And the great surprise is what happens before he gets to say it.

teach.b: It's in Luke, chapter fifteen, the third in a row of stories about lost things: a lost sheep, a lost coin, a lost son. A man has two sons.
The younger asks for his share of the inheritance now, while his father is still alive. Some readers hear in that something close to: I wish you were dead.
The father gives it. He goes to a far country and spends it all. Famine comes, and he ends up feeding pigs, so hungry he'd have eaten their food.
Then, in the King James words, "when he came to himself." He will go home and say: I've sinned; I'm not worthy to be your son; take me on as a hired worker. He rehearses it.

teach.h: THE FATHER SAW HIM, AND RAN.
teach.b: Here's the verse the story turns on: "But when he was yet a great way off, his father saw him, and had compassion, and ran, and fell on his neck, and kissed him."

Some readers take the far-off seeing to mean he'd been watching the road. Some commentators note that grown men of standing rarely ran in public. The son starts his speech, and never reaches the hired-worker part.

Bring the best robe, a ring, shoes; kill the fattened calf. "For this my son was dead, and is alive again; he was lost, and is found." But the older son, out in the field, is furious the waster gets a party.
And the father goes out to him too. The story never says if the older brother comes in. Christians read the father as a picture of God's welcome.
The door is open for both sons.

how: Christians read the parable of the prodigal son as a picture of God's welcome to anyone who returns, and it is read often in churches, especially in seasons of repentance such as Lent.

o: sorry, full of regret for what you did
unusually gifted, like a child genius
wasteful, spending everything without a care

games.q: who did what in the story — tap the pairs.
p: saw him far off, and ran

s: the word prodigal appears in Luke's story
the title came later. the King James says he wasted his substance.
the father ran to the son before the apology was finished
he saw him a great way off, ran, and embraced him.
the story tells us whether the older brother joins the party
it ends with the father's plea, and leaves it open.

games.q: you're the father. your son, who wasted everything, is a speck far down the road. what do you do?
o: wait at the door to hear his apology
run to him and embrace him
send a servant to ask what he wants
games.why: he runs, falls on his neck and kisses him, and calls for the robe, the ring and the fattened calf before the apology is done.

practice: Bring to mind someone who's drifted from you, or let you down, or you've been waiting to hear from, and picture them far off down a road; notice whether your heart tightens or leans forward.
You don't have to decide anything; just picture taking one step toward them, before any apology is finished. If the one who drifted is you, picture someone watching the road for you.

wordCard.voice: Prodigal, Latin for wasteful: the son who wasted everything and came home, and the father who saw him a long way off, and ran.

orig.note: Latin: lavish, wasteful. the source of English prodigal; Luke's Greek says the son lived wastefully.

carryVoice: Your line: he ran. The father didn't even wait for the speech. Eighty-three days in.

sources.q: But when he was yet a great way off, his father saw him, and had compassion, and ran, and fell on his neck, and kissed him.
For this my son was dead, and is alive again; he was lost, and is found.
